talks.title: TROOPERS24: Keynote
talks.teaser: Demonstrates keynote - A question of time and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Industry Evolution and Tooling

Keynote speaker Guillaume Arcas of Google Mandiant Flare reflects on TROOPERS' history and warns newcomers against over-relying on current tools. Fundamentals matter when tooling fails—past tools like w32dasm disappeared, and even IDA faces uncertain futures.

AI Limitations

He tested feeding a modified malware decryption algorithm to AI, which returned a confident but wrong answer without doubt. AI adds a new factor to the attacker-defender game, but human expertise and skepticism remain essential.

Learning Through Failure

Arcas advocates embracing mistakes and uncertainty as normal learning steps, rejecting cultures that punish failure or idolize flawless experts. Education systems wrongly glorify top performers while dismissing those who repeat grades.

Individual Expertise

Everyone possesses unique knowledge others lack. His first conference talk came after realizing colleagues overestimated what others already knew—a lesson about connecting outside one's bubble to recognize personal value.

talks.title: The Red Teamer’s Guide to Deception
talks.teaser: Analyzes the Red Teamers Guide to Deception and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Why Red Teams Still Win

Balazár and colleagues from SBS red teaming show real engagement shells and walk through cases—telecom Linux lateral movement, financial password spraying to core banking, and manufacturing AD attacks—where detections fired but failed to evict attackers.

SOC Reality

They argue SOC teams struggle with incomplete log coverage, noisy legacy tools mimicking attacker behavior, alert fatigue, and analysts who lack domain context. Determined attackers retry until they slip through sparse medium-severity alerts.

Internal Honeypots as Smoke Detectors

The speakers advocate cheap internal deception: fake credentials, canary hosts, and tripwires that almost never false-positive because legitimate users never touch them. Alerts warrant senior analyst response and slow attackers who must question every vulnerability.

Vendor Case Study Caution

A deployed commercial deception product on all laptops failed when the team entered via a non-laptop vector and never triggered embedded tokens. Their lesson: simple, environment-tailored honeypots with admin buy-in beat over-engineered rollouts.

talks.title: Fuzzing at Mach Speed: Uncovering IPC Vulnerabilities on MacOS
talks.teaser: Reviews fuzzing at Mach Speed: Uncovering IPC Vulnerabilities on MacOS and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Speaker and audience

Mandiant/Google consultant Dylan Frankie presents year-long research on fuzzing macOS Mach IPC, aimed at offensive researchers and defensive engineers alike.

Fuzzing basics

Fuzzing sends unexpected inputs through attack vectors to trigger crashes in memory-unsafe C/C++ code, potentially exposing buffer overflows, use-after-free, and similar bugs.

Approach

He contrasts mutation-based fuzzing (mutating valid inputs) with grammar-based fuzzing, focusing on mutation for this work. The fuzzing cycle is his framework for finding and refining memory-corruption issues.

macOS IPC focus

The XNU Mach layer handles low-level IPC. Mach ports act as kernel-managed mailboxes; services register with the bootstrap server (e.g., com.apple.Troopers) so clients can allocate ports, register services, and exchange messages. He argues base Mach IPC is a high-value target because many higher-level mechanisms build on it.

talks.title: How to travel the C SAFely with .json when there are no Argonauts
talks.teaser: Details how to travel the C SAFely with .json when there are no Argonauts and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Dina from Germany's BSI maps coordinated vulnerability disclosure onto the myth of Jason and the Argonauts, using CSAF JSON advisories as the modern "fleece" that helps researchers and vendors navigate disclosure safely.

## The Disclosure Problem
Reporting a vulnerability feels like encountering an unknown "Minotaur": unclear policies, missing security.txt files, and fear of legal or professional retaliation. She contrasts manufacturer-centric "responsible" disclosure with coordinated disclosure mediated by neutral bodies.

## CSAF and BSI's Role
CSAF provides machine-readable JSON for security advisories, enabling automation across government and industry. BSI acts as Medea—holding the fleece, brokering public advisories at the end of CVD, and shielding researchers when vendors push back.

## Takeaways
Organizations should publish security.txt, adopt CSAF, and treat coordinated disclosure as a shared journey—not a back-room negotiation.

talks.title: Analyzing and Executing ADCS Attack Paths with BloodHound
talks.teaser: Analyzes analyzing and Executing ADCS Attack Paths with BloodHound and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Andy Robbins (co-creator of BloodHound and Principal Product Architect at SpecterOps) and Jonas (Product Architect at SpecterOps) explore the identification, analysis, and execution of Active Directory Certificate Services (ADCS) attack paths using BloodHound. Following the foundational research in the "Certified Pre-Owned" white paper by Will Schroeder and Lee Christensen, the speakers explain how ADCS abuse primitives can allow unauthorized domain or enterprise privilege escalation, how these paths emerge through combinations of configurations and privileges, how BloodHound visualizes and models them, and practical strategies for auditing and remediation.

### Key Topics
- **ESC1 Abuse and Modeling**: ESC1 occurs when a certificate template permits a subject alternative name (SAN) supplied by an enrollee (allowing impersonation of high-privilege accounts like domain admins) and has an Extended Key Usage (EKU) valid for authentication (such as Client Authentication). In BloodHound, this is represented by an attack path directing to the domain head, which can be unfurled via the "composition" view to examine the required templates, Enterprise CAs, root trust, and enrollment access rights.
- **ESC3 (Enrollment Agent Abuse)**: ESC3 involves requesting a certificate from a template containing the Certificate Request Agent EKU, which allows the holder to act as an enrollment agent and enroll on behalf of other users (such as target domain admins) in another template. BloodHound models this with an `enroll on behalf of` relationship between templates.
- **ESC5 (ADCS LDAP Object Manipulation)**: ESC5 encompasses misconfigurations and write privileges over securable Active Directory LDAP objects tied to ADCS (e.g., within the Public Key Services container in the configuration naming context, such as Certification Authorities and the `NTAuthCertificates` store). Missing prerequisites can be substituted with existing access permissions. The speakers detail how generic write/create privileges over these containers permit an attacker to fully bootstrap a rogue CA into Active Directory, even in environments where ADCS was never installed, enabling escalation from domain admin to Enterprise Admin across forest boundaries.
- **ESC13 (Issuance Policies & OID Group Links)**: Abuse of certificate templates specifying issuance policies linked via OIDs to universal groups (such as Enterprise Admins or Enterprise Key Admins), granting Kerberos ticket group membership upon authentication without explicit static group membership.
- **Visualizing and Auditing PKI Hierarchies**: Using BloodHound's graph visualization and API (supported in both BloodHound Community Edition and Enterprise) to map PKI trust, identify non-tier-0 accounts with control over ADCS objects, and discover insecure template configurations.

### Technical Details
- **ESC1 and ESC3 Tooling**: Demos utilized `Certify` to request certificates with specified SANs or enrollment agent permissions, Windows `certutil` for formatting PFX files, and `Rubeus` to request Kerberos TGTs into memory, as well as extracting NTLM hashes.
- **Bootstrapping Rogue CAs (ESC5)**: Exploiting `GenericAll` on the `Certification Authorities` container and `NTAuthCertificates` object. A self-signed CA CRT and CRL are published using `certutil -dspublish`. A lightweight HTTP server serves the CRL so domain controllers can complete validation when the DC processes the newly trusted root via Group Policy (which refreshes every 5 minutes by default).
- **Forest Boundary Crossings**: Because the configuration naming context replica is writable on domain controllers when running as `SYSTEM` (which possesses an ACE on the container), child domain admins can modify forest-wide configuration objects, bypassing standard trust separation.

### Takeaways
- **Audit ADCS Object Control**: Rights like `GenericAll`, `WriteDacl`, or `WriteOwner` on public key services containers should strictly belong to Tier-0 principals.
- **Remediating ESC1**: Restrict enrollment permissions on templates with `ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT` exclusively to Tier-0 identities, or remove authentication EKUs.
- **Securing Enrollment Agents**: When smart card enrollment or help desk delegation is required, implement explicit enrollment agent restrictions on the Enterprise CA to strictly define or deny which templates and principals can be targeted.

talks.title: Exploiting Token-Based Authentication: Attacking and Defending Identities in the 2020s.
talks.teaser: Outlines exploiting Token-Based Authentication: Attacking and Defending Identities in the 2020s and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Overview
Dr. Nima, Principal Identity Security Researcher at Microsoft's Threat Intelligence Center, delivered a comprehensive talk on exploiting token-based authentication systems. The presentation covers both historical context and modern federated identity architectures, demonstrating practical attacks and defensive techniques.

Evolution of Authentication Models
The talk contrasts two paradigms: the legacy silo model where users authenticate directly to each service (creating multiple credentials and single points of failure), and the modern federated model where a centralized Identity Provider (IDP) issues tokens for use across multiple Service Providers. The federated approach reduces risk by isolating identity credentials from individual service providers.

Authentication Protocols and Token Types
The speaker traces three major federated protocols: Kerberos (since 1989), SAML (2002), and OAuth 2.0/OpenID Connect (2007). Modern implementations typically use JWT (JSON Web Tokens) consisting of header, payload (claims), and signature. Entra ID uses ID tokens and access tokens (1-hour lifetime) and refresh tokens (90-day lifetime). Bearer tokens are credentials where possession alone proves identity without requiring cryptographic proof of possession.

Attack Taxonomy
The speaker presents a two-pronged attack model: (1) stealing tokens directly from users or systems, or (2) stealing signing secrets from IDPs to forge fraudulent tokens. Attacks map to MITRE ATT&CK techniques including T1552.04 (unsecured credential storage for private keys), T1528 (steal web credentials), and T1550.001 (access token manipulation). Stealing secrets enables longer-term, broader attacks (impersonating any user), while token theft provides temporary access bounded by token lifetime.

Live Demonstrations
The speaker demonstrated extracting JWT access tokens from browser developer tools (F12) and using them to query Microsoft Graph API endpoints. Additional demos showed: (1) forging Kerberos service tickets using stolen domain controller secrets, (2) creating fraudulent SAML tokens by signing them with stolen certificates, and (3) extracting claims from ID tokens using online JWT decoders. The speaker's custom PowerShell toolkit enabled complete exploitation workflows.

Real-World Case Study: Storm-0558
The April-July 2023 attack by Chinese threat actor Storm-0558 exemplifies the severity of secret theft. The actors compromised an expired Microsoft account token signing key and exploited an Exchange Online misconfiguration to access emails from approximately 25 organizations. The attack was detected through careful correlation: activity appeared in Exchange Online unified audit logs with no corresponding Entra ID signing events, indicating token forgery.

Detection Strategies
Effective detection requires coordination across multiple log sources. For hybrid identity environments: correlate on-premises domain controller logon events with ADFS audit logs and Entra ID signing logs—any resource access requires corresponding authentication events. For cloud-only identity: monitor for Entra ID signing events with no corresponding user authentication, indicating forged tokens. IP validation: extract and compare IP addresses from ID/access tokens against actual request source IPs in application logs. The speaker demonstrated custom code comparing token IP claims with request IPs to detect token theft, though this requires custom application instrumentation. Optional claims (IP address, user agent) added to tokens enable forensic comparison.

Prevention Measures
Layered defenses include: (1) harden IDP components to Tier 0 status, (2) use custom certificates and Hardware Security Modules (HSM) for private key storage, (3) enforce zero trust policies restricting access to managed, compliant devices only, (4) implement token binding (emerging technology) to cryptographically bind tokens to client devices, and (5) enable Continuous Access Evaluation for real-time revocation. Zero trust prevents token theft by limiting access to corporate resources only from managed endpoints.

Emerging Technologies
Token binding and Continuous Access Evaluation represent protocol-level improvements not yet universally standardized, aiming to prevent token use outside legitimate contexts. The speaker noted these are technical advancements but lack universal standards.

Takeaways
Token-based authentication security depends on protecting secrets (stored in HSM, access-restricted) and tokens (encrypted in transit, validated on use). Defending against sophisticated adversaries requires correlating authentication logs across endpoints, IDPs, and service providers. The Storm-0558 case demonstrates that even major organizations can suffer token signing key compromise; detection through log correlation proved critical. The speaker emphasized this is a team sport requiring both infrastructure hardening by administrators and custom detection mechanisms from developers.
